title: WHY THE ECONOMY IS A HOUSE OF CARDS…IN AN EARTHQUAKE ZONE
label: human
full_text: CUTTING THE CARD QUICKLY, HAROLD EDGERTON, 1964 I. HOW LONG CAN IT LAST? How long can it last? The world is in crisis. Much of it, caused by America’s President. And yet the US economy is “booming.” Is it? I think it’s a house of cards. The US economy today is often called “K-shaped,” meaning that there’s a class of people who are doing well, and a class that aren’t. So far, so predatory capitalism. It’s a pretty…simplistic…metaphor. It has no dynamics, no interactions, no inner structure at all. That’s why I think it’s lacking . This frame hides a number of crucial — and catastrophic — realities. A much better metaphor is a house of cards. How we see social realities matters, if we want to understand — and be able to predict — them. Let me explain. II. THE CRUCIAL WEAKNESS OF THE US ECONOMY, OR, MONEY MONEY MONEY The US economy has an Achilles Heel. A critical weakness. It’s 70% consumption. That means that it’s exquisitely sensitive to changes in consumption, which is how much people spend (versus invest, and we’ll come to the investment part shortly.) This is unique, different, and a true point of critical weakness. It’s unique in the world. No other economy on the globe consumes at such a high rate. It’s different from the rest of the wealthy world, too, which is much more sensitive to changes in government investment, because of the expansive social contracts in Europe and Canada. And it’s a true critical weakness in the sense that a small, unforeseen change can wreak absolute havoc. It can cause failure cascades. Like those in 2008, where banks failed, or in 2003, where the dot com bubble crashed, or during the pandemic, where the economy went haywire. So: the US economy depends critically on consumption, which is also why the news about it is always about how much other people spend, and that’s deeply weird if you’ve ever lived overseas. And if that number falls, even a little bit, then the economy can go south, fast, hard, and deep, unlike almost anywhere else in the world, too. III. THE THREE MAGIC NUMBERS IN THE ECONOMY What is an economy? Let’s think of it as a set of markets. Stock markets. Bond markets. Currency markets. The labor market. And so on. There are more, but those will do for now. What happens when this Magic Number, consumption, begins to falter, even just a little bit, in America? One almost elementary consequence is that the stock market falls. The bond market weakens, too. So does the currency. And of course, eventually, labor markets do too, meaning that unemployment begins to rise, which is easy to understand if people are buying and spending less. Now we’re going to begin discussing the house of cards metaphor a little. America, like I said, is unlike any other economy. Not just because everything depends on Magic Number One, consumption. But also because that Magic Number determines Magic Number Two, the stock market. Magic Number Three, by the way, is GDP, which depends on the first two. The stock market in America is everything. People obsess over it unlike anywhere else in the world. Europeans and Canadians by and large have no idea what their stock markets are doing, and that’s because they don’t have to care: they don’t have these miserable things called 401Ks. Investment and retirement’s taken care of for them. But in America, Magic Number One, consumption, determines Magic Number Two, the stock market, or people’s 401Ks, savings, etcetera, which is everything . The stock market in America is everything in a literal sense. Europeans and Canadians have expansive social contracts, like I said, from retirement to healthcare to childcare. In America, you work, and your money’s put into the stock market more or less automatically. The stock market is the only safety net there is. It has taken the place of every single functional system in working countries . That’s why Americans obsess over it, and they’re right to, they have to. No money, you die. Now think again of the link between Magic Number One, consumption, and Magic Number Two, the stock market. See how America’s always on edge about the economy? That’s because the economy is always on the edge. It’s on a perpetual knife edge. A tiny move in the wrong direction can have life-wrecking consequences. Even for “rich” Americans. V. THE CLASS STRUCTURE OF AMERICAN WEALTH Now let’s picture the house of cards. The K shape metaphor says: richer Americans are doing well. And it implies that they’ll continue to do well. We imagine the branches or legs of the K having their own momentum, separating, bifurcating. But is that true? “Richer” Americans these days have grown wealthy largely due to a single industry: tech. It’s provided a route to the upper middle class, what’s left of it, through astronomical salaries and stock market gains. So much so that Americans now make 3–4 times what their counterparts do in the rest of the rich world. Does that sound sustainable to you? I digress a little bit. My wife and I were in Seattle recently. I was astounded by the level of wealth a little bit. Nice shops, restaurants, cafes, with astronomical prices, tiny houses that cost a fortune. So I did a little research, and learned something I didn’t know before. Seattle has the largest number of tech workers in the country . Hence, all this newfound wealth. “Tech,” we’ve discussed recently, is misnomer. It’s really advertising, and mail order. They’re responsible for a very, very large portion of this K shape. And the story goes like this. This class of richer Americans will just keep spending, spending, spending. So there’s an idea that “the wealthy can just keep spending…forever.” But will they? Can they? Maybe if their money came from the heavens above, certainly. But the wrinkle in this very earthly tale is that their money is coming from below, because they are in the business of mass advertising. Global, in fact, and the world economy is emphatically not doing well. However you look at it, their wealth comes from the rungs of the ladder below them. Once you understand that this is a story of advertising , then things become much clearer. To advertise, you need people in mass, society-scale, markets to buy stuff. Who can . If they don’t, then of course, there’s little reason to advertise. So while it’s true that these richer Americans may want to keep spending, the point is that they’re employed in and by an industry which depends on advertising to everyone else . Not just them. This is how the US economy really works right now, and has for a decade plus. See what I mean by house of cards a little bit? VI. THE HOUSE OF CARDS Now let’s put it all together. This new class of techno-wealthy, and here I don’t mean Musk and Bezos, but your average tech worker pulling a quarter of a million plus, is working in an industry — advertising — that’s premised on selling ever more stuff to the people below them in the economic ladder. That is where their wealth is really coming from. And they’re one step away from catastrophe, too, make no mistake. One lost job, one missed paycheck. This level of wealth doesn’t insulate you much at all from the brutal realities of American financial life — that comes with having tens or hundreds of millions. At this level of wealth, family, groceries, and housing are still very much an ongoing basic issue of household financial management. To put it another way, this level of the house of cards is fragile. It’s not on solid ground. It depends critically on the one beneath it. Now think of the other stratum beneath them on the economic ladder. How are they doing? The ones being advertised to ? Not very well at all. They’re under immense strain. They are struggling to make ends meet, and we see it in every statistic there is, from bad debt, to rising credit card delinquencies, to car payments, to savings rates, to levels of distress, and so on. Magic Number One, Two, Three. See how much risk they’re at? Of… VII. WHAT HAPPENS TO A HOUSE OF CARDS? What happens in a house of cards? The bottom falls out. The bottom layer suddenly gives way, and the rest of the thing collapses as if it were nothing at all. A breeze blowing the wrong way undoes it. This is where the economy really is. And I think that the “K shape” metaphor hides this. Prevents us from really seeing it or understanding it well. If we think about it clearly, a house of cards is a clearer pattern for us. It has internal structure, dynamics, logic, the elements are related, and there is a pattern to it at the macro scale. It isn’t just “some cards are doing well, and others aren’t.” None of the levels of such a house are safe, on solid ground, secure. Let me continue my little explanation. Remember Magic Numbers One and Two? Consumption and the stock market? What happens if the bottom begins to give way, and the people at the bottom stratum stop spending at what are now rates they can barely, if at all, afford? The rung above them feels the pain instantly, and in multiple ways. Their jobs, created by advertising, are at sudden risk (and I won’t even get into AI for now.) And so is their wealth, which is tied up in the stock market, and locked into stock options of the very “tech” meaning ad companies they work for. They face a triple whammy. So there are feedback effects here, which make the edifice a house of cards: unstable by its very nature . All this is why Americans are under so much financial stress and pressure, too, no matter what rung of the economic ladder they’re at. Everything is poised to fall apart, perpetually and constantly. Precisely because nothing is on solid ground. Every rung of the economic ladder above is sitting above one that’s precarious and unstable and shaky, and so the economy just stays unstable the further you go up, perhaps even more so. This is why you see the interesting and morbid effect of couples making a quarter to a half a million dollars a year jointly, which is an amount the entire rest of the world would be flabbergasted by, and who still “feel poor.” If you make it to the very top, which is to say, you made hundreds of millions, or dozens maybe, you can jump off the whole damned thing, buy a yacht, and sail away. But until then? You’re still trapped in it all. VIII. A HOUSE OF CARDS IN AN EARTHQUAKE ZONE Now think of all the shocks heading our way as a world. Trump started a foolish war that’s causing an energy crisis that’s going to cause a massive inflationary wave. The economy worldwide is stagnating. People are getting sick of tech and it’s weird man-child obsession with controlling their lives in puerile ways. Climate change. Fascism. Etcetera. AI, ripping away all those jobs from this tech meaning advertising class, and replacing them with idiot sales bots. Any one of those alone would be enough to cause the house of cards to teeter and sway in the wind. But all of them together ? I think of the US economy as a house of cards standing on an earthquake zone. Was that a rumble I just heard? I’d be very, very careful about where you invest your wealth these days. Wise investment isn’t about catching the breeze. It’s about foundations, resting on solid ground. Love, Umair (and Snowy!) http://www.umairhaque.org WHY THE ECONOMY IS A HOUSE OF CARDS…IN AN EARTHQUAKE ZONE was originally published in Eudaimonia and Co on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: The Fairy Door
label: human
full_text: The magic we build for our children, and what remains after it breaks. The fairy door the at the base of our oak tree Piper sat on her knees in a chair, focused on two little scraps of parchment on the table in front of her, a rainbow of colored pencils scattered about. One was a note left by fairies in our backyard. The other was blank and waiting for her reply. Every time Piper bent over the paper, her hair fell into her eyes. She brushed it back and kept printing in careful block letters. She was writing back. My wife and I stood there watching while she worked. She kept stopping to think, then adding another line. Her tongue pushed out a little when she concentrated. She pressed hard enough with the pencil that the letters had to be visible on the back. She was writing to somebody real. That was plain. That night, after Piper was asleep, Nancy and I stood at the kitchen counter with glitter on our hands and a pile of tiny junk from Michael’s spread out between us trying to decide what Misty, our backyard fairy, should say back, and what gift she should leave for Piper. A bead. A button. A fake jewel. A little earring. Tiny scraps of paper. Tulle. Lace. Little bags. Scissors. Glitter on the laminate, glitter on the faucet, glitter somehow on our shirts. Nancy held up a tiny spoon and asked whether it was the sort of thing Misty would gift. I had no idea, but I nodded anyway, lost in the note Nancy had written in miniature, amazed at how easily her handwriting passed for something from another world. Outside the kitchen door, the old oak stood in the dark, the little wooden fairy door we’d bought at a craft store glued low against the trunk. My wife tied the spoon to the note with a ribbon, propped it against the door, and slipped our daughter’s letter into her pocket. Those nights still sit near the top of the list when I think about being a parent. The first door went into that old oak maybe three feet from the side-yard door off our kitchen, close enough that the kids could discover it when playing the yard, but hidden enough so the discovery felt like theirs. The tree was enormous and older than the house by decades. Maybe a century. Its branches sprawled across most of the yard and down the hill, and its trunk was so thick that a child could easily imagine a world inside. The second door was in the stone wall, half hidden behind tall dry grass just to the left of a rose bush, tucked low in the mulch with a tiny mailbox outside that we found at the craft store. A fairy with a pen pal needs somewhere to receive letters, after all. One fairy door was a surprise. Two was a neighborhood. But Nancy and I were smart enough to stop at two. And we learned that while the fairy in the oak was a homebody, the ones in the wall were frequently on vacation — there are only so many notes a parent can write after all. Piper left letters at both, and the fairy that was home wrote back. We never gave either door an official street number, but they might as well have been 419 and a half and 419 and three-quarters. The fairy door in our garden wall. During that summer, Piper left drawings, coins, marbles, little plastic animals. Anything she cared about enough to give to a small friend she came to love. She asked the fairies about their lives and told them about hers. Misty mattered. Her brother was in the story, too, though not the same way. Piper went all the way in. She named them, wrote to them, worried about them. Max was younger, but somehow more suspicious, which put him in prime position to push on the magic door and see whether it moved. He was, as far as any five-year-old can be, a happy skeptic. At the time, I didn’t think about what any of this meant. Nancy and I didn’t stand at the kitchen counter with glitter on our hands discussing child development projects. We did the types of things parents do all the time. We wanted to make the world bigger for our children, but also small enough that they could matter inside it. It’s part of the job. We make rituals and games. We tell stories and make up fairy tales. We hide eggs. We fill stockings. We don’t always know what lasts and don’t know what will feel magical or foolish. Most of the time we’re just hoping. That, I think, is one of the harder parts of being a parent. You’re always putting things into your kids’ lives without any guarantee of where it lives in them ten years later. Stories and traditions. Rules and responsibilities. Sometimes a tiny brown fairy door glued near the root ball of an oak. At the time, you’re not standing there thinking about the future. You’re thinking about the children in front of you. The one kneeling at oak tree and the other trying to see behind the door. You’re thinking about notes to Misty in careful block letters written at the table where you would later craft the perfect response, sprinkled with pixie dust. Whether you’re trying to make their world larger or warmer, or simply more fun, I’m not sure. But it’s from love. Years later, I was in my office reading an essay by a Substack author named Sophia ( I used to believe in magic ) about growing up with fairies and finding out her mother had been behind them all along. At this time, Piper was two and a half hours away in her first year of college, probably taking notes in her stats class, tongue still poking out in concentration. She was a long way from the girl at our kitchen table with parchment and colored pencils spread out in front of her, but not as far as time would suggest. Then I hit the line in Sophia’s essay where she wrote she had been angry, that she had felt fooled by her mother, and the whole thing came back in a rush. The door in the oak tree. The other one in the stone wall behind the tall grass next to the rose bush. The little mailbox. The glitter near the sink. Piper kneeling by the roots, her note waiting to be answered. And with it came a question I had managed not to ask when the kids were little. What had we actually given her? And I immediately thought about the day the door came off the tree. Max pried it loose. We told him it was sealed by magic, so I don’t know if he expected it to come off or open up. But when Piper ran into the house crying that Max was trying to break the fairy door, I ran outside to find him using a spoon to lever it loose. It came off as I came out, and he held to door up toward me with a mix of shock and pride. The back of the door showed plain wood and glue with no sign of magic or another world. I took the door from Max and told him to go inside. I glued it back on. I made up something about the power of fairy magic, and hoped for the best. After that, Piper wrote another note. Dear fairies, I’m sorry Max broke your door. Love, Piper. This one was all words, no drawings. No hearts. You could see her hope fighting with reality in the note. A child who thought her brother damaged a fairy house sat down and tried to make it right. She wanted the fairies to know she was sorry. She wanted them to read it. She wanted them to know she meant it. She wanted them to be real. But could that magic hold? In hindsight, the door was always going to come off sooner or later. What my wife and I never gave much thought to was what would happen to the magic once the fairies were gone. We never pictured Piper looking back on the notes or the gifts or the apology and feeling stupid for caring that much. We saw the notes as evidence of sincerity, not something she might one day have to laugh off as an embarrassment. Eventually Piper stopped writing the notes and the fairies gave way to other things. Tea parties. Card games. Hide-and-seek. School. Friends. The small, crowded life of a child getting older. For Nancy and me, the transition felt easy enough. We didn’t spend much time wondering what happened to all that feeling when the notes stopped. We certainly didn’t ask whether what we’d given her was more wound than wonder. Then Sophia’s essay raised that same question, years later. She wrote that she felt like a fool when she found out her fairies weren’t real. She had been upset at her mother for a long time, but later came to understand that maybe magic was real all along because of what her mother created and how she made it real. That last part is what I hadn’t thought about. I had no trouble remembering the enchantment, and I still felt the injury, but I never knew whether the injury was the end of it. And that’s the reality of parenting. You’re almost never working with certainty. You’re working with hope and your best judgment, making choices that feel loving in the moment, and trusting time will prove you right. And sometimes you are, but sometimes you’re not. Sometimes something you meant to be magic turns out to be a craft store door glued onto a tree. You don’t always know the impact of your choices. Sophia’s essay put Piper back in front of me. My wife and I had built a world in the yard and watched our daughter step into it. All the way into it. She wrote to the fairies and left them gifts. She wrote to Misty the way you write to somebody you expect to answer. So what had we done? Had we given her a beautiful childhood memory, or had we built an early heartbreak with glitter and ribbon and a glue gun? When I picture Piper at that table, bent over the parchment with her hair falling into her eyes, I don’t think about a child being tricked. I think about a child learning to imagine life on the other side of the door. She wrote to Misty. She left gifts by the roots. When Max broke the door, she sat down and wrote the fairies an apology in careful block letters. I can’t find much wrong in that. But the answer here belongs to Piper. I can tell you what I remember building, what I worried about later, and how I feel about it now. But what it felt like on the other side of that fairy door is hers to say, just as it was Sophia’s. So, I went to my bedroom and opened the little wooden box in my dresser. I pushed aside the bent paper-clip people Max made for me, a couple of Nerf darts long separated from their gun, a beat-up Pokémon card, some frayed ribbons, a few Play-Doh figurines, and, for reasons I still can’t explain, a Ziploc bag full of baby teeth. Near the bottom was a small piece of parchment, the letters in pencil pressed hard enough to be visible on the back. I knew what it was before I unfolded it. I took a picture and sent it to Piper and asked, in the careful, over-serious way a parent asks when they are not quite sure whether they did the right thing, whether making that world for her had felt like magic, or like being fooled. After a few minutes, her answer bubbled up on my screen, and it was simpler than my worry. She remembered it sweetly. She obviously knew plenty of childhood magic was made by adults. Santa. The Easter Bunny. All the little worlds parents build and children enter until they are old enough to see the seams. The fairy doors, to her, were not an injury doused in glitter. They were fun. They were ours. She was glad we put them there. So I sat there alone with the note in my hand and thought about the girl at the table, and the daughter I have now. I thought about the old oak, the stone wall, the little wooden door, the tiny mailbox, the spoon tied on with ribbon, the glitter on the counter, my wife writing in miniature because our daughter believed somebody small and hidden might be glad to find it. And I sat there with the message she just sent, and felt glad she had that world for a while. For a long time, I thought the magic ended when the notes stopped. Now, I know better. The magic never had to end, because it was never the world behind the fairy door, it was that she knew to look for one in the first place. The Fairy Door was originally published in Human Parts on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: On shoehorning your hobby into your job (no, it won’t kill your passion)
label: human
full_text: You can monetize your passion Photo by Steve Johnson on Unsplash For many people, our jobs are not our source of joy and passion. (I mean, mine is today. But it wasn’t always like that.) We do our work, and then we come home and do whatever it is that drives us and fulfills us. We read books, we crochet, we write. That’s a healthy work-life balance. This myth was what I erroneously believed when I finally started taking my passion of writing seriously. I wanted to find time for it; I realized I had to make time for it. I would come home from work and write for half an hour every day before dinner. That didn’t work, so I decided to try getting up half an hour earlier and finding time for writing then. That also didn’t work — I found myself unable to prioritize it, hitting the snooze button instead. I tried different schedules, habit trackers, and methods of finding time in the corners of my day to work on my writing. None of them stuck. The problem was deeper: My energy levels were not conducive to passion projects on the side. Fresh out of grad school, at my first 9–5 job, I found myself shocked by how tired I was. No matter how much I intended to start working on my novel, I’d somehow find myself booting up Sims or scrolling Facebook instead — or just staying asleep. When you’re tired, it’s much, much harder to follow your passion, even if it’s something you love and care about. Creative pursuits require brainpower. If you’re exhausted by your job, it’s just that much harder to make that time. Here’s how I managed to find time for my passion project after all — with some tweaks to the game plan. Find the common ground I thought my job (customer service) and my passion (writing) had nothing in common. I was wrong. Writing is in almost every single job. You write emails, you write Slack messages, you write summaries of projects. All of it is writing. But none of that felt like super creative writing. I wish I could say I forced myself into a solution, but the truth is I stumbled upon an answer by accident one day in my customer service job. I was getting many questions about the same new feature (product recommendations) from our customer base. I had already copy-pasted our corporate jargon answer what felt like a zillion times in Zendesk. Finally, I got fed up and wrote up a more friendly, helpful how-to about the new feature, published it on our company blog, and started linking people to that instead. (That night, I woke up in a cold sweat because my manager had not okayed it — I spoke with her about it the next day and thankfully she was fine with it, but I recommend you confirm with your managers first if it’s OK!) That was just the start — there were many other places my writing passion fit As time went on, I discovered multiple ways to incorporate more writing into my job. I wrote up product launches, FAQs, thought leadership, and even ghostwrote a few LinkedIn posts for our CEO. I pitched my manager on hosting recorded workshops for our customers, too. Ultimately, writing at work didn’t compete at all with my job— it made me better and more effective. And it was fun. I loved thinking about what our customers would likely need, and putting together resources to help them do that. The only surprise was that I pivoted to non-fiction. Though I’d always thought I wanted to be a novelist, and I still do, I found an unexpected joy and love in writing nonfiction Following my passion at work led to a passion-filled job The best part is that finding time for writing at work led me to my current job as a product storyteller at Medium. I spent years creating guides, developing resources, and hosting workshops at my customer support job, as a freelancer, and as a content creator. Ultimately, that experience led me to be uniquely qualified for the job I have now, which I adore. Dodge the issue of monetizing your hobby Another benefit: this approach allows you to avoid the classic burnout of trying to make money from your job. When you love something and try to add a pricetag, it can often drain the passion out of your passion project, bogging you down in the minutiae of trying to run a business or make a buck. But by doing it the other way around — make money by bringing your passion into your day job — you can keep the passion alive. And if you feel it slipping? Scale back and focus on your core duties until you’re ready to pick it back up again. Final thoughts If you’re low on time and struggling to prioritize your writing hobby, find a way to work it into your job. You may be surprised by what doors it opens. P.S. I completed this story as part of the Just Start Writing challenge hosted by Medium in June 2025. It’s not perfect, but it’s done!

title: You Do Not Need To Fully Understand Yourself To Feel Better
label: human
full_text: Give your “research” a rest Photo by zaid noori All too often, our efforts at “self-improvement” in the realms of happiness, love, and emotional wellbeing begin (and end) with “analysis.” We think that the right approach to feeling better is “understanding” what’s wrong, and why. We consume content, pore over resources (of varying degrees of credibility), learn the big words and the explanations, and intellectualize the hell out of everything we must be experiencing (after all, it’s right here on paper saying so.) This feels good - in the moment. “Rabbit-holing” always feels good. It soothes a specific anxiety that will have us wholly convinced it is the path out of this mess; that “reason” and “explanation” feel good because they seem like progress. But in reality, they are only fueling our anxiety, not actually resolving or touching any underlying states, which is why it quickly becomes so compulsive, never-ending, and exhaustive. At the end of the day, we don’t feel better. We feel strung out, wired, “informed” and “soothed” in an immediate sense, on the surface, but still strung out beneath the surface, all the underlying, important things left without contact. The way to feel better Is not to intellectualize, label, or analyze, but to actually feel the things we are avoiding when we do things like this. To be aware of the uncomfortable rising up and swelling of anxiety — to notice it and allow it, rather than scramble to feed its demands with more information in an effort to appease it and “make it go away.” To experience the sharp pang or hollow pull of sadness. To feel the heaviness in our shoulders of stress, the ache in our lower backs of financial worries, the restlessness in our legs as we lay down in bed, struggling to find a position that will resolve it. The way to feel better is to feel these things. It’s counterintuitive, and directly contradicts everything we do, and the internal messaging we get around them (to varying degrees of volume, intensity, and insistence.) The way to feel better is to acknowledge small things as they come up throughout our day. Because as we become more familiar and accustomed to smaller things, instead of explaining them away or externalizing them in other explanations (of what he or she did, or “why” we are the way we are), we afford ourselves the opportunity to exist as full humans, and the space to actually breathe and experience different emotional energies, which is the entire baseline of feeling comfortable in our own skin; i.e., feeling good.

title: Your Emotions Don’t Need The Right Word
label: human
full_text: You can identify what you’re feeling without the vernacular Photo by Fons Heijnsbroek I genuinely have no idea where people come by their emotional vocabulary. My best guess is that it’s taught to some people by their parents during early attunement (e.g., a child loses a toy and the parent reflects, “you must feel so sad”), but on the few occasions I’ve asked people with children whether this is the case, I haven’t gotten clear or consistent answers. This leaves the next likely possibility that we pick them up through seeing others express emotions and then hearing them name them. We see someone crying, for example, and then hear them say, “I feel so sad.” The challenge with both of these is that they are building an internal map based on external surveying. Either: Someone else ascribing a word to what we feel, and then we, in the absence of having a better word handy, feel as though we’re in a position to accept that this must indeed be the hat for it. Someone else describing their internal state and labeling it, and we, in the absence of our own internal gridwork, accept that when something looks and acts like this, it must be the same word. Both of these leave us without our own understanding of what we’re experiencing, instead relying on a language that may not match. And while, in a sense, this is how much language works (and really, most of society, including social norms, financial structures, and institutions, with us collectively agreeing that concept x is called x and means x ), when it comes to the realm of own lived experience, vernacular like this may not ever actually reflect what we’re feeling. And then some part of us is left standing outside the exchange. There is often pressure to package up the complexity of our experience neatly. But when the signals are layered, fragmented, dynamic and changing, and in various states of vagueness, volume or oscillation, to do is in fact not to “connect” with anyone, or ourselves, at all, but rather cheapen the experience, and cut it down to something pocket-sized, handy, and easy to hold, hand over, receive, and then drop. But human experiences don’t actually work like that. The reason we so often struggle to know what we’re feeling is because what we’re feeling can’t be wrangled into simple terms . Humans are complex creatures. We do not “experience” in primary colors. To understand how we feel, the solution is not a feelings wheel (though they are cool), nor is it a tighter understanding of emotional language (though it can be helpful.) The solution to understanding how we feel is in opening up all the doors and windows on our full linguistic capacity. It’s exploring everything we know about the language we speak, even beyond “reasonable” or conventional connections and associations. Instead of “sad,” it’s saying what it really is , which is probably something more like: “everything is gray and quiet,” or “I feel like I’m wearing a coat the size of a duvet and the weight of a house,” or, as Teddy Roosevelt wrote in his diary on Valentine’s Day 1884, when both his wife and mother died the same day: “the light has gone out in my life,” written under a simple, articulate: “ X .” Instead of “happy,” we might feel like we did “on the first ride with a new bike as a kid,” or “I can’t stop smiling,” or “I feel so warm, light, and lit up.” We could cheapen this to “happy,” but to do so is to strip away the vibrance of what we were actually feeling, before we rinsed it through a single word. Why does this matter? Because this is how we truly experience emotions. To speak in genuine and layered, fragmented, or implicit emotional language is to truly see them, and the only way in which we truly see and experience ourselves to know how we feel and, just as importantly: it’s also the only way in which we can be truly seen by someone else. To speak in forced simple terms is to leave ourselves outside of the dialogue. To speak as we actually feel, at times vague or layered or fragmented or indirect, is to share what we truly feel and truly connect.

title: What’s The Point Of A Relationship?
label: human
full_text: It depends on who you ask Photo by Xhiliana There are a lot of different ways to approach relationships, many of them normalized, not all of them great. Conventionally, the social structures around relationships (i.e., marriage) were a matter of social status, stability, and security. And to some degree, we’ve maintained this storyline in much of how we approach love. Even if the marriage rate is lower, and individuals do not need to enter into marriage in order to have access to resources, it still provides the backbone of many relationships. For many, relationships are also a haven in which to build an identity and a container in which to structure our sense of self (and ego, in the psychological sense) through the ways in which it is contrast to another. If we have a gentle partner, we can look strong. Or, conversely, we want to appear a certain way and so we find a partner that echoes those values. Also very normal. For others, we enter into relationships to subconsciously aggravate unknown wounds , dredging them back up, unknowingly, in hopes of resolving them. We fall in love with our shadows, our secrets, the things within ourselves that go bump in the night, and end up resenting each other in search of resolving something that actually lives inside us. For some, it also simply provides some buffer against the fear of dying alone , a very human anxiety. There is, of course, a more compassionate approach to love , wherein the purpose of a relationship is: simply to practice love. To receive and support each other as human beings and bear witness to who they are, moment to moment and across their lives. This framework, of course, requires something different of us; a looser grip on relational expectations around how our partner represents us or meets the unresolved pains we call “needs.” The approach also requires both people to actually be in touch with who they are. Because without this knowing, there is nothing to share, nothing to witness, nothing to offer to have loved, or love in exchange (leaving those within the relationship falling back to one of the other patterns in its place.) If we want compassionate love, where we enter into relationships with the lens of them serving as vessels purely to love one another in close regard (which is admittedly not for everyone, as it contradicts many other, more conventional and common approaches), then we have to be prepared to offer the “meat” for the potluck to exchange. To have compassionate relationships, built on the goal of simply loving one another, we have to first love ourselves enough to sit with and experience our emotions, deeply, while resisting the urge to either dismiss them or delegate them to others / things outside of us to resolve. To love compassionately, and love another for the full fabric of their being and offer our own in return, requires us to first know the full fabric of what we experience day to day, and many of us do not exist in that mental model. It can be built, however, with small simple attunements to anything and everything that comes up for you in a day (and there are countless, layered, often conflicting things.) When we build an intimate and comfortable familiarity with all of the details of what makes us up, we are better equipped to actually relate to others in order to offer ours, and receive theirs with equal compassion.

title: In the Sea in Her Dress
label: human
full_text: She climbed out of a window at sixteen to marry the man her parents had refused. My grandmother, Antigone. The car smells of cigarettes and four children. It is Sunday morning again, which means all six of us will load ourselves into the car and my father will drive us to my grandmother’s house in Larnaca, on the southeastern coast of Cyprus. My three brothers and I are squashed together in the back seat, each of us fighting for territory. No one wants the middle. The middle belongs to the smallest one, which means it always belongs to me. My father smokes as he drives. The window on his side is rolled down and the cigarette smoke is carried out of the insides of the car. In the winter, the windows stay shut and he smokes anyway. None of us thinks to complain. It is the late seventies, maybe the early eighties, and children breathe in whatever their fathers smoke. The road from Nicosia to Larnaca is straight and flat and uninteresting, and it takes an hour to get there. Every Sunday we pass the same dry fields, the same unfinished buildings just sitting under the searing heat. My brothers fight over a comic book. My mother turns around every so often to tell them to stop. My father drives away with one hand on the wheel, a slight squint in his eyes, and a cigarette dangling between the fingers of the other hand, listening to the crackle of the radio. I’m at the front edge of the seat with my hands holding the sides of my parents’ seats and staring at the road ahead from the windshield. Eventually, the blue of the sea flashes between the bends, and all four of us begin chanting, “There’s the sea! There’s the sea!” When we pull into the yard, the door is open before we are even out of the car. My grandmother is there, waiting with her arms open for our arrival. Her name is Antigone. She lives in a house in Larnaca that the state gave her after the war. The house belonged to a Turkish Cypriot family who was displaced in the other direction in 1974. Somewhere in the north, other families are living in the houses Greek Cypriots left behind. This happened without consent, without agreement. My grandmother carried what she could salvage from her life and made this house hers. She planted trees in the yard and she raised chickens. The house is a very basic one. Across the yard stood a small structure, and that was the bathroom. Inside, the walls are plain. The kitchen is a small room with an old table and a few chairs and a stove that has seen many long winters. Religious icons hang on one wall; such is the usual decoration of every Cypriot grandmother’s house of that generation. There are a couple of framed photographs, her husband and her when they were young with their six children, when everyone was still alive. Her husband died before the war. One of her sons died too, both of them taken by heart attacks in their thirties and forties. By the time she lost her house in Famagusta, she had already lost two of the people that were meant to grow old, there, in that house, beside her. She points to the photographs sometimes when we ask questions, and she tells us stories about what her husband and son were like, in a gentle voice. The dead are in the room and they are loved and they are not weighing it down. She also tells us about her elopement. She is sixteen, or seventeen, or perhaps eighteen; the age changes depending on the telling. Her parents have refused her the man she has chosen. He is from a different village, not the match her parents were imagining for her. She does not accept their refusal. She climbs out of a window to meet him. He is steadying a donkey. She mounts behind him, and they ride fifteen kilometres down the mountain. They don’t come back until they are married. By the time her parents see her again she is my grandfather’s wife, and he is the one she chose, and the choice cannot be undone. She tells this story sitting at the kitchen table, holding our hands or pinching our cheeks, smiling at our faces as we listen. “You are my treasures,” she tells us, “You are beautiful and clever and the most beloved children in the world.” I don’t have to do anything to earn my grandmother’s love. The love is not contingent on the cleanliness of my hair or the quietness of my voice or the tidiness of my room. The love is there, when I walk through the door, it is there while I’m eating, while I’m playing in the yard, it is there when I make a mess, and it is still there when I walk out the door. I am six, or seven, or eight, and I think every grandmother is like this. She is not like every grandmother. In the summers my parents drive me down on a Sunday and pick me up the following Sunday. The mornings begin in the yard. She is already awake before I am. Sometimes I find her in the kitchen having her coffee; other times, she is in the chicken-shed at the back, collecting the eggs the hens have laid during the night. There are five or six chickens inside a wire-mesh coop roofed with corrugated metal. Their enclosure smells of straw and feathers. She lets me go in with her and shows me how to lift a hen gently to see if there is an egg under her. The eggs are warm when you find them, warm in a way eggs from a fridge never are. I carry them out, cupped in my hands, two at a time, as though they are small living creatures. We have them for breakfast, fried in olive oil with bread. The yolks are a deep orange from whatever the chickens feed on in the yard. She pours me a glass of milk and watches me eat with the kind of attention that is the centre of her love. She is not watching to monitor me. Watching me is simply what she most wants to do, so she does it. After breakfast we go to the sea, which is a hundred metres from her front door. We walk down the narrow road, my hand in hers, until it opens onto the beach. The beach is a strip with large, grey pebbles, with no umbrella or kiosk. My grandmother doesn’t know how to swim. She’s a Cypriot woman of her generation who spent the first decades of her life inland and the rest beside the Mediterranean, and nobody ever considered teaching her how to swim. She doesn’t let this stop her. She walks into the sea in her dress. A cotton black dress, falling below her knees, is what she always wears. She doesn’t have a swimming costume. The water creeps slowly up the dress until it reaches her thighs, and there she stops. She stands in the sea with the dress floating around her legs, the saltwater darkens the cotton, while she watches me swim further out and back again toward her. I splash her and she lets me. She laughs and doesn’t make a move to resist my playfulness. When I’m ready to come out she walks out beside me. With our bare feet on the protruding pebbles, we put on our flip flops and go back to the road towards the house. We arrive and she hangs her dripping dress in the yard to dry and changes into another one before she makes lunch. This is a day spent with my grandmother, and there are many like it. They are all roughly the same. Nothing happens in any of them, and that sameness is the gift; there is only a grandmother and a child in a yard with chickens, and the sea down the road. Meals appear at regular hours, and the afternoons pass under the trees she planted to turn a house into a home. She tells me stories about her childhood, her early married life in Varosha, the seafront town of Famagusta, full of people before 1974, hotels along the front, before everything was lost. She tells me about my grandfather and how he made her laugh, how he was young and alive. She tells me about the elopement, again. Then she tells me about the war in 1974, how she packed what she could in a few hours and left, never to return. I don’t remember her telling me that my grandfather fought in Greece during the Second World War. I do remember her telling me that she still has the key to the house in Varosha. No family was ever moved to her house. She tells me how the army put a fence around the town and let no one back, a whole town with no one living in it, the buildings still where their owners left them. These things aren’t told in a sorrowful tone. The losses exist in the narration of her life, but they are not the heart of it. When I’m back home in Nicosia, in my mother’s spotless kitchen, with its angled cushions and sterile floors, I do not consciously compare the two women. I only know that the air feels different in my grandmother’s house, that she says things no one else says to me, and that when I sit at her table, nothing is being asked of me. My mother loves me. I have said this and I will say it again. My mother loves me in the register she has, with meticulous hair, unblemished rooms, driving me to lessons, never saying she is proud. The two women learned different steps to the same dance. What I understood then was that some Sundays we drove to Larnaca and the door opened and the woman who lived inside was excited to see me, and that she said so with words and with the way she watched me eat. That woman gave me something I could not name and could not get anywhere else. She gave it to me freely. From the sea off Protaras, where I sometimes swim these days, I can see Varosha. Ten kilometres across the water the town is still standing, the tall hotels along the coast, and nothing moving. I swim out and look at it. Somewhere inside that silence is my grandmother’s house, behind the fence, and the door her key opened. She is in the sea in her dress. I’m ten metres out, swimming back to her. Her dress is dark with the wet, and her silver hair is uncovered, left to dampen in the salty air. She is squinting at me against the sun. She is, in this moment, exactly herself. She’s the girl who climbed out through a window for love; the woman who buried a husband and a son; the refugee who walked out of Varosha carrying what she could; the old lady who planted trees and raised chickens and stands in the sea in her dress because the sea is there, and she cannot swim, but she will not be kept out of it. She’s also my grandmother. And now she is standing there, watching, waiting for me to swim back to her. title: The Cabin
label: human
full_text: PERSONAL REFLECTION A meditation on duty, heritage, and the walls we build to stay safe Photo by Maria Ilves on Unsplash Friend link here . I live in a cabin. This cabin is built with my thoughts and powered by a Worry Hearth in the middle of its one-room building. This is not a cabin where people retire for pleasure or rest and relaxation. This is a cabin entirely made to imprison, because I am confined by my circumstances — my illness, my filial piety, and my sense of duty to my partner, children, and the home and household we have built together. The foundation of this cabin is built on the way I was brought up. The teachings of Confucius and Daoism form the fabric of how my family took care of their own — 2,500-year-old traditions ingrained into the fibres of our identities, including the importance of ancestral veneration and respecting our elders. This brings a sense of obligation, a paralyzing guilt that will follow if I were to walk away. I told my partner when we married that my parents could come live with us; that was my condition for our marriage. The floors of this cabin are laid with my resilience. I came to this country located halfway around the world from the only home I knew. I was just a kid with one suitcase, armed with my parents’ money and blessings. The smooth floors under my bare feet are reminders of where I came from and the lovely life that I have built with my partner. These floors used to be rough, even sharp; shaped by racism, discrimination, and humiliation. These floors were worn smooth by our sacrifices and determination. The walls of this cabin are built from my sense of obligation to my family. Can I do right by them? Every day, we wash these walls down with rituals — this is the business of living. My health, my caregiving responsibilities to everyone else, whatever leftover time I have, this is mine. Some days I am exhausted mentally by just the completion of this washing. I shouldn’t complain because these are the moments that remind me of my existence — that I still have a heartbeat and that I am healthy enough to care for everyone. Then we move to the Hearth. This Worry Hearth is powered by my anxieties. Every day, there are new things to feed it. I gravitated to a career that allowed for control and organization, so the twigs and logs we throw into this fire are not just about my health, my family, or my career. It is also the worry of how to structure, plan, and organize our lives. I can generate a roaring fire some days from just planning something mundane and inconsequential. The glow from this fire is reflected back on my family as I gaze proudly at them. The roof of this cabin is made from my protective tendencies — the bear parent. If you mess with my family, it’s personal. I don’t like starting a fight, but I will sure help you end it. These protective tendencies, unfortunately, block the stars, preventing my family from growing wings and soaring high. It does, however, keep them safe and takes fuel away from my Worry Hearth. Lastly, the windows. Everyone tells me to have a bucket list. I don’t want one. Instead, I see everyone else’s bucket list through my windows. I am content inside my privileged life, having this little cabin where I can observe vicariously and risk-free. As I watch through these windows, I weave. Using my creativity, I craft tapestries for my walls. I now have more tapestries than can fit on my walls, but I still go on — the process of weaving gives me joy, not the display. So, these tapestries occupy a large box in this cabin, a hidden archive of my imagination. I live in a cabin. This cabin shelters me and provides me with the comfort I need. The warmth I get from my Worry Hearth is not just a source of stress, but a source of energy to keep going. This cabin, completely built by my own thoughts, is not just my prison — it liberates me from the cruel outside world. title: Being Dramatic Is Not The Same As Feeling Deeply
label: human
full_text: On the contrary: the two are often in conflict Photo by Michael & Diane Weidner There is a spectrum to the ways in which humans will handle their emotions, from “very expressive” at one end, to very subdued at the other. Expressive individuals may fold their energy into emotional language, amplifying it because they feel something, and by creating action and output around that, it invites a moment for others to “turn towards” in return. It makes the energy look and seem as though it must be proportionally, “bigly” true. Expression and feeling are not synonymous. But very often, externalized emotions are not being felt, they are simply being broadcasted as means for connection and feeling seen and heard as a person (though they may also identify as those feelings.) But the performative nature of the expression is intensified not because it is necessarily felt more strongly, but because their resistance to feeling it is stronger. To express dramatically is fundamentally to externalize . Very often, emotionally expressive and loud individuals do so not because it proportionately reflects deeper feelings, but rather a more prominent unease with being alone with whatever feelings they have. To feel is first fundamentally internal. And to feel deeply is often very quiet work. It requires that the focus be turned toward, not out (whether that’s expression or rumination, e.g., whatever “they” did.) To feel anything at all, we need moments to let things catch up with us, to snag on our attention, to have space on the shelf of our awareness. Contrary to some frameworks, this does not necessitate carving out whole stretches of time, or learning to meditate, or “finding a quiet space.” You can do it at any moment. We have flickers and fragments and layers of feelings all the time. It’s just a matter of being aware of them, of noticing the lightning bug of a flash in our psyche as something moves across our tertiary awareness. And we can share afterwards, if we choose, of course. The real benefit here being that if we do the internal part first, whatever we share is a much more authentic expression of our selves .

title: Why I Thank the Universe Every Time I’m Triggered
label: human
full_text: The pain you run from is the very thing trying to set you free Image Source: Getty Images Rain tapped against the window in a rhythm that felt louder than it should. I sat curled in the corner, a mug of half-cooled coffee in my hands, scrolling through my phone. Mostly doomscrolling, if I’m honest. One by one, I skimmed through comments on recent posts. Most were harmless. A few were kind. But then my eyes snagged on a sentence that felt heavier than all the rest. It wasn’t the first mean comment I’ve ever received. And it won’t be the last. We live in a world where people feel free to say whatever they want about you, especially when they can hide behind a screen. Most of the time, I brush it off. I remind myself I’ve done the work. That I know who I am. That I don’t need strangers to validate me. But this one was different. It found me in a vulnerable moment. I was tired, stretched thin and less centered than usual. And in that split second, the words sank deep. They pulled me straight back into old wounds, old stories, old insecurities I thought I’d buried. That’s how triggers work. They don’t knock politely at the door. They break it open. And they don’t care how “tough” you are. My chest tightened. My jaw locked. The words rippled outward, stirring something I thought I had buried years ago. I kept scrolling, pretending I wasn’t bothered, but my body told the truth. My pulse quickened. My mind spun. My coffee went cold in my hands as the comment replayed on loop. And in that quiet room, with nothing but rain for company, I realized that this wasn’t about the comment at all. It was about me. About all the times I had believed I needed to be enough. Thought I had to be seen to be loved. And about the loneliness that said told me maybe I’m still not. I walked across the carpet, tracing the familiar pattern with my eyes, trying to ground myself. I could taste the sharp tang of guilt, the acrid sting of inadequacy. And beneath it all, a deeper ache, one I recognized but had hoped was gone. When the Shadow Whispers Carl Jung said: “Until you make the unconscious conscious, it will direct your life and you will call it fate.” Eckhart Tolle names this the pain-body, an accumulation of unresolved hurt waiting for a match to flare. Rumi poetically reframes the sting as something tender: “The wound is the place where the Light enters you.” What if that tiny fracture in my chest was not evidence of brokenness, but the crack through which something greater might emerge? Into the Wound Let me tell you about how triggers feel. Imagine you’re walking through a dim forest. The path is familiar, the air cool, earthy. You’re steady, present. Suddenly, you step into a patch of quicksand. It’s not deep at first, but you’re sinking. Little by little, panic seeps in. That’s what a trigger does. It drags you into the past, into stories you told yourself a thousand times: I’m not enough. I’m unlovable. I won’t be held. You reel, trying to escape. But the harder you struggle, the deeper you sink. Traditionally, we fall into three scripts: fight, flight, or freeze. We lash out, we avoid, or we collapse inside. In that moment by the window, I wanted to do all three. But instead, as my heart slowed, against my instincts, I paused. I named it: This is shame. I pressed my hand to my chest, as if comforting a child. And I whispered, quiet, shaky, but true “ Thank you”. It felt absurd. Pain doesn’t feel like gratitude. But in that trembling moment, I understood the trigger wasn’t cruelty. It was a calling. A Practice Born from Pain Since then, I’ve woven a ritual into the broken parts of my day. When the hurt arrives: Pause. I stop rushing. I breathe into the tightness. I give myself space to feel. Name it. “This is shame. This is longing. This is fear of rejection.” Trace it. I ask, “Where have I felt this before?” More often than not, it’s childhood. It’s old rejections, repeated stories, unspoken needs. Thank it. “Thank you for showing me what still needs healing.” It’s not denial. It’s wisdom acknowledging its own wounds. Choose again. I respond with softness where I once reacted with armor. I speak softly. I set boundaries kindly. I breathe through the grief. Nothing transforms overnight. But over time, the wound softens. The pain becomes wisdom, the ache becomes awareness. The quicksand loosens its grip. A Lotus Grows in Mud There’s a Buddhist metaphor that teaches us that the lotus grows from the mud yet blooms unafraid. Its beauty is inseparable from the murk. Without the mud, there is no bloom. In my life, the triggers are the mud. The bruises, the voices of fear, the stories I whispered in darkness. And my healing, the flowering of self-compassion, clarity, and peace, only happens when I lean into the mud, instead of running from it. Triggers don’t mean we’re broken. They mean there’s more to heal. They’re not punishments. They’re invitations to softness, to truth, to reclamation. A New Relationship with Pain I will never outgrow triggers. Nor should I. To be human is to carry wounds. But what I’m learning is that I can change my relationship to them. I’ve stopped fighting the cracks in myself. Instead, I kneel before them. I press my palm into the rough edges. I see the child behind the hurt, still needing love. I breathe into the tear. Because that’s where light gets in. So if you feel triggered, tonight, tomorrow morning, in a room where the silence grows teeth, don’t hide from it. Stay. Sit. And ask: “What is this pain trying to teach me?” Let the quiet answer. Let your breath be the bridge. Let the pain be the portal. Because beneath the ache is your teacher. And through the crack, your healing begins. title: Better Virtual Meetings Start with a Pro Setup: Try These 8 Tips
label: human
full_text: Even if your teams have returned to the office, I’m guessing virtual meetings are still a significant aspect of group collaboration and communication. Sometimes it’s still the best way to gather a distributed team for productive collaboration! Leading through screens is hard work, but getting your tech set-up right is going to make the process infinitely smoother and, more importantly, lead to better results. Over the past six years of facilitating virtual sessions, I’ve learned something important: the quality of a virtual workshop often starts with your setup. When you’re running a virtual session — especially if you’re doing it solo — you’re likely thinking about holding the room, guiding decisions, and keeping people engaged across screens and time zones . It’s not about nailing a Pinterest aesthetic — it’s about having the right tools to lead smoothly and confidently. Here are eight pro-tips that make a huge difference. 1. Dual monitors are a must When you only have one screen, you’re constantly toggling between: The collaboration board Participant reactions The group chat An agenda That friction pulls your attention away from the group. With two monitors, you can do a better job of staying present while also quietly managing the flow behind the scenes. I keep my virtual collaboration tool, like Miro, on the big screen, with the agenda and chat on the second screen. This might seem like a small thing, but it changes everything. 2. Keep participants’ faces visible In a physical space, you can naturally read the room. But virtual facilitation requires us to recreate that awareness intentionally . That’s why I put the toolbar with participant faces at the top of my big monitor, right above the Miro board. This will help you: Read reactions and body language See when someone wants to jump in Notice confusion or hesitation Seeing faces helps you maintain something close to virtual eye contact , which keeps participants engaged and reminds them they’re part of a real conversation, not just another meeting window. 3. Hide self-view if it distracts you Watching yourself can pull your attention into performance mode instead of curiosity mode (more on that, here ). Your job is to guide the conversation, not critique your own facial expressions. Personally, I usually hide my self-view because I feel like it ends up being a distraction and is not helpful for fostering connection and engagement. 4. Use Post-it notes, even during virtual sessions When you’re leading a virtual meeting or workshop, you’re juggling listening with synthesizing, and guiding with capturing. It’s a lot! One thing that can help with this is to use a stack of physical Post-its to: Quickly capture ideas or themes while participants are talking Read them back to the group Confirm alignment Transfer ideas onto the Miro board It’s a simple way to stay mentally organized while conversations move quickly . 5. Keep a few things nearby that help regulate your energy Facilitating a workshop — even a virtual one — takes real energy. I keep a few small things nearby that help me stay centered, like a nice-smelling candle, or a cool stone I can hold during intense discussions. This might sound a little unconventional, but good facilitation is about managing the room’s energy . And that starts with managing your own. When you’re calm and grounded, the group usually follows. 6. Lighting matters more than you think Natural light is great, but it doesn’t always work with desk placement. Good lighting helps in a few ways: Participants can clearly see your expressions You look more present and engaged The overall session feels more professional When your setup looks thoughtful, participants subconsciously feel that the session itself will be thoughtful too . Pro tip: I use Hue lights above and in front of my desk so I can tweak the lighting depending on the time of day. 7. An external camera can make a big difference Being able to position the camera exactly where it works best helps create a more natural conversational angle instead of the classic laptop “looking down at you” view. Right now, I’m using a Logitech MX Brio. The biggest benefit isn’t just image quality, it’s camera placement . Again, it’s a small detail that improves human connection through the screen . 8. Keep your beverages handy This sounds minor, but it prevents those awkward moments where you have to pause the session to get up or reset . I keep my hydration station on the right so it’s easy to sip coffee or water without interrupting the flow of conversation. Small logistics matter when you’re facilitating a room of people whose calendars are tightly packed. Good facilitation is often about creating more ease and preventing tiny disruptions before they happen . Why a Solid Setup Is Worth It You might wonder if all this setup is overkill. But here’s the reality: virtual collaboration already starts with a disadvantage compared to being in the same room. People are distracted. Attention is fragmented. Energy is harder to maintain. A strong facilitation setup helps close that gap and allows you to: Read the room more effectively Guide discussions without fumbling with tools Maintain credibility and presence Respect everyone’s time It’s about creating the conditions for clear thinking, productive collaboration, and forward momentum . And those outcomes are worth a little extra effort before the meeting starts. I’ll leave you with one final thought: wearing the leadership hat and the facilitator hat at the same time is HARD. Leadership requires judgment and direction. Facilitation requires neutrality and mechanics. When one person tackles both simultaneously, progress can suffer. If your sessions feel heavy, unbalanced, or exhausting, it may be a role overload. Check out this post to see why this is so hard, and when you might want to bring in reinforcements. title: You Are The Authority On Your Own Feelings
label: human
full_text: They‘re yours Photo by Artists Eyes Sometimes we feel uncomfortable or unclear emotions, or are vaguely uncomfortable with the landscapes of our inner experience, and it’s very common in these moments to seek help; a friend, a partner, a parent, a therapist, a framework, a tool. And while these may seem helpful in the moment, the goal is not for anyone (or anything) outside of yourself to “tell you how you feel.” While individuals may indeed do this, and it often happens as an attempt at a co-regulation gesture (i.e., one of soothing), the act undermines the relationship with our own internal experiences. Someone else stepping in as the authority on your feelings is akin to helping a butterfly out of its cocoon. It will perish. “Helping a butterfly out of its cocoon (or chrysalis) often permanently dooms it. The physical struggle to emerge forces vital fluids from the insect’s abdomen into its wings. Bypassing this process leaves the butterfly with a swollen body and shrivelled wings, rendering it permanently unable to fly.” While it may feel nice to be “free of the cocoon,” and for someone else to “help you” do the emotional toiling effort (especially someone who seems to have a more robust emotional vernacular, or is in a position of authority (such as a therapist), or a piece of software), this can be detrimental in the longterm. While you may now have a word, a gaze, a receipt, you lack the skillset by which to actually feel the full fabric of the thing and understand it more dynamically, especially as it relates to you and other emotions. The goal of these conversations, and tools, is not to “tell you how you feel,” or “give you a result,” or “tell you the answer.” The healthiest conversations about our feelings are often not the ones where someone explains us to ourselves. They are the ones where another person helps us remain present long enough to discover something on our own. It’s about shared presence and non-judgmental understanding, not labeling, explaining, answer, or fixing. Nobody else can actually verify your feelings. They can suggest, reflect, wonder, hypothesize, resonate, disagree even… but they cannot know. A therapist cannot know. A framework cannot know. AI cannot know. A partner cannot know. At best, they can help you look. The container of a relationship, framework, or tool used in a healthy capacity is meant to be a safe space to explore emotional terrain, not the how-to guide of trails to stay on. Our work is finding the footing, feeling around, fumbling, dealing in fragments and fuzziness. And this work is as essential to the human condition as emerging from the cocoon is to the butterfly. Feeling complete in our capacity and experience requires us to beat against our internal awareness ourselves. The person who ultimately gets to decide what your experience is remains you.

title: Certainty Is for Dead Things
label: human
full_text: The sun on the balcony of my little town in the Alps reheats my cold coffee. Being in the presence of these mountains already feels like being with old friends. I know their full names. I have seen them act moody and shy, hide behind a cloth of dense fog, or crave attention by showing off their snowy beauty. I’m here for a writer’s residency for a month. It feels like a clear invitation to, well, write. These words are for you, dear reader. I do, in fact, live inside a postcard. The past months have been full of invitations. Some arrived as intriguing synchronicities, some as gentle intuitive impulses, others as sudden, sharp slaps. Narratives shifted. Certainties melted. People exited my life in dramatic ways, making space for delicious new adventures. A few weeks ago, I wouldn’t have been able to access this perspective — to see the blessing in apparent destruction. To see it as an opportunity to start again, to create on the fertile soil of collapse. And yet, here I am, spiraling again around the wisdom of paradoxes. The deepest heartbreaks alongside the most miraculous openings. Desolation and destruction coexist with vibrant aliveness — seeds sprout after a forest fire. We are capable of breathtaking beauty and atrocious acts. We survive the unthinkable and create beauty with what remains. 𒀭 What would it mean to fully embrace (y)our own contradictions? 𒀭 How do you hold space for the messy wisdom of paradoxes? Maybe these contrasts don’t take away from life’s beauty, but actually expand our capacity to be more present with what’s real. This is what makes us human. Our paradoxical nature is part of being alive. When we accept complexity and messiness — both in ourselves and in others — we begin to relate to life, rather than resist it. Nuance becomes possible. So does deep, lasting change. Still, it’s tempting to wish for a simpler world. I see this impulse everywhere — the desire to make things neat and clear, to sort life into tidy divisions. It’s understandable — simplicity feels safe, coherent, controllable. But these divisions exist only in theory, in the fantasy of control. That’s why I see it as a radical act to celebrate contradictions, to stay with unresolved tension long enough for nuance to emerge, to bloom into something messy, unexpected, true. Only dead things are certain. Everything alive dances in varying degrees of uncertainty. May we enjoy the dance. With a sense of wild possibility, Laura This article was originally published on my Substack newsletter. If you want to receive these pieces directly, you can subscribe here.
